To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) BRAF mutations are frequent and prognostic in unselected metastasis patients, 2) BRAF mutations do not explain all poor prognostic patients, 3) patients not given chemotherapy have very short survival and 4) TMA availability is an important under-exposed issue.
BRAF mutation is an important factor for prognosis and treatment selection in mCRC and that many mCRC patients have a very poor prognosis.

1) the BRAF mutation is more common than previously reported in mCRC, and is an independent prognostic factor, 2) BRAF mutation is a poor prognostic factor regardless of MSI status and 3) survival in mCRC is very variable and subgroups with extremely short survival exist, and these subgroups are not well represented in the present clinical trials.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the prognosis in unselected patients with metastatic colorectal carcinoma varies from 26 months in patients with wildtype KRAS and BRAF, to 1 month in patients with BRAF mutation and no treatment.
BRAF mutations are associated with poor survival in mCRC, but that the impact is not as large as in other cancers.

KRAS/BRAFs status and TMA availability are important prognostic factors in mCRC, and that BRAF mutated patients should be offered anti-epidermal growth factor receptor treatment, but that the prognosis of many patients remains poor despite the best treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prognosis of mCRC patients varies widely, and the most important prognostic factors are age, performance status and BRAF mutation.
the prognosis of mCRC patients is extremely variable, and we lack knowledge about the worst cases, which is an important issue when designing future clinical trials.
we need to be aware of the heterogeneity and poor survival of mCRC patients, and that the lack of available tissue for molecular studies may lead to a biased view of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be aware of the fact that we have a very heterogeneous group of mCRC patients, with very different survival.
the prognosis of metastatic CRC patients varies considerably and that the biologically worst cases are not represented in clinical trials.

the observed 21% mutation frequency of BRAF in mCRC is higher than the repeatedly reported frequency of 5-10%, and this should be considered in clinical practice when BRAF mutation is used as an exclusion criterion for treatment with anti-EGFR antibodies.
